summary:
The Satellite-Based Land Surface Temperature Trend & Anomaly Explorer is an interactive web platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” It transforms NASA Terra MODIS satellite observations into accessible visualizations and scientific insights, helping users investigate Earth's land surface temperature patterns over time.

Using daytime Land Surface Temperature data from 2020 to 2025, we examine three contrasting environments: George Town, Malaysia; the Amazon Forest, Brazil; and the Sahara Desert, Algeria. We apply harmonic regression with HAC robust statistics to estimate temperature trends while accounting for seasonal variation. An AI-assisted anomaly screening module also identifies unusual observations for further investigation.

The platform enables users to explore regional trends, visualize satellite observations, investigate anomaly candidates and analyse their own CSV datasets. By combining satellite data, statistical analysis and interactive technology, our project makes Earth observation more accessible and encourages scientific curiosity and evidence-based environmental investigation.
details:
A. What does the project do and how does it work?

The Satellite-Based Land Surface Temperature Trend & Anomaly Explorer is a browser-based scientific investigation platform that helps users explore Earth's land surface temperature patterns using satellite observations.

The project uses NASA Terra MODIS MOD11A2.061, focusing on daytime Land Surface Temperature (LST), together with its quality-control information. The study covers 26 February 2020 to 27 December 2025.

We selected three geographically and environmentally contrasting study regions:

  • George Town, Malaysia: An urban and coastal environment.
  • Amazon Forest, Brazil: A tropical forest environment.
  • Sahara Desert, Algeria: A desert environment.

These regions provide different environmental contexts for examining and comparing land surface temperature patterns.

Our platform works through three main stages:

1. Satellite Data Exploration

Satellite observations are processed using Google Earth Engine to obtain regional temperature time series. Quality-control information is considered when evaluating the observations.

The website presents the processed information through interactive charts, allowing users to explore temperature changes across the study period and compare different environmental regions.

2. Statistical Trend Analysis

We apply harmonic regression with Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent (HAC) robust standard errors to estimate temperature trends while accounting for recurring seasonal patterns.

The analysis produces trend estimates and 95% confidence intervals, providing users with a statistical basis for investigating changes rather than relying only on visual impressions.

Our estimated trends are:

  • George Town: −0.5533 °C/year.
  • Amazon Forest: −0.1490 °C/year.
  • Sahara Desert: −1.2453 °C/year.

These values represent fitted trends over the approximately six-year study period. They should not be interpreted as proof of climate change causation or as evidence of a particular environmental cause.

3. AI-Assisted Anomaly Detection

The project incorporates an anomaly screening method based on seasonal-trend residual analysis.

A harmonic regression baseline is used to represent expected temperature patterns. Observations are then assessed using robust residual scores. An observation is flagged as an anomaly candidate when:

abs(robust_z) >= 3.5

The screening uses 2020–2023 for training, 2024 for validation and 2025 as a holdout period.

The detected candidates are presented for further investigation. They are not treated as confirmed environmental events, and we do not claim model accuracy or predictive performance without appropriate validation.

B. What makes the project innovative?

The main innovation is the integration of satellite data exploration, statistical trend analysis and AI-assisted anomaly screening into one accessible web platform.

Instead of simply displaying satellite images or isolated temperature measurements, the project allows users to follow temperature observations over several years, examine fitted trends, understand seasonal variation and identify unusual observations that may deserve further investigation.

The website also supports user CSV uploads and browser-based analysis. This allows users to explore their own datasets rather than being restricted to the three original study regions.

By combining data visualization with scientific investigation, the platform encourages users to move beyond looking at charts and begin asking meaningful questions about Earth's changing systems.

C. What are the benefits and intended impact?

The project aims to make satellite-derived environmental information easier to access, understand and investigate.

Its intended benefits include:

  • Environmental awareness: Helps users explore land surface temperature patterns across different environments.
  • Scientific education: Demonstrates how satellite observations and statistical methods can be used to investigate environmental trends.
  • Accessible data exploration: Makes complex scientific datasets more understandable through interactive charts and visualizations.
  • Evidence-based investigation: Encourages users to question unusual observations, consider data quality and interpret statistical results responsibly.
  • Adaptability: Allows users to upload their own CSV datasets for additional exploratory analysis.

Our long-term vision is to expand the platform with more satellite datasets, additional environmental indicators and a wider range of geographical study regions. This could create opportunities for broader Earth system investigations and environmental education.

D. What tools and technologies were used?

The project combines Earth observation technology, scientific computing and web development.

Satellite data and processing

  • NASA Terra MODIS MOD11A2.061 – Daytime Land Surface Temperature and quality-control data.
  • Google Earth Engine – Satellite data processing and regional data extraction.

Scientific analysis

  • Python – Statistical analysis, harmonic regression and anomaly screening.
  • HAC robust standard errors – Statistical uncertainty estimation.

Website development

  • HTML and CSS – Website structure and interface design.
  • JavaScript – Interactive browser-based functionality.
  • Plotly – Interactive scientific charts and visualizations.
  • PapaParse – CSV parsing and user dataset uploads.

Cloud and development tools

  • Azure Static Web Apps – Website hosting.
  • Azure Functions v4 with .NET 10 Isolated – Backend submission functionality prototype.
  • Azure Blob Storage – Submission data storage prototype.
  • Docker and Azurite – Local backend development and testing.
  • Visual Studio – Development environment.

The backend submission workflow has been successfully tested locally using Docker and Azurite. Public cloud deployment remains a future development task and is not presented as a completed feature.

E. What factors did the team consider?

Scientific reliability, data quality and responsible interpretation were important considerations throughout the project.

We considered the following factors:

  • Data quality: Satellite observations may contain missing or lower-quality measurements, so quality-control information is important.
  • Seasonality: Temperature patterns naturally vary over time. Harmonic regression helps account for recurring seasonal variation when estimating trends.
  • Spatial coverage: The amount of valid spatial data can vary between observations and should be considered when interpreting results.
  • Study duration: The analysis covers approximately six years, which limits the conclusions that can be drawn about long-term environmental change.
  • Anomaly interpretation: Unusual observations are screening candidates that require further investigation, not automatically confirmed environmental events.
  • Scientific responsibility: Statistical trends alone cannot establish climate change causation or identify the environmental processes responsible for observed changes.
  • Accessibility: The website was designed to make scientific information easier to explore without requiring users to have advanced programming or statistical knowledge.

Ultimately, our goal is not to claim that an algorithm can explain every environmental change. Instead, we developed a tool that helps people explore satellite evidence, trace temperature patterns, investigate unusual observations and develop better scientific questions about Earth's systems.
